Extraction: AIDR-Cloud: An Agentic AI-Driven Incident Response Framework for Cloud Failures (title page, p. 1).

Akshay Pratinav and Archana Kataria, both affiliated with Intuit Inc, Mountain View, USA (p. 1) — an industry-authored paper, with the reference implementation deployed on the authors' own multi-region serverless environment (§IV, p. 3).
2026, SoutheastCon 2026 (IEEE SOUTHEASTCON conference series), proceedings pp. 163-168, DOI 10.1109/SOUTHEASTCON63549.2026.11476571 (p. 1, footer).

Modern cloud-native systems (hundreds of microservices, multi-region Kubernetes, Kafka streaming pipelines) have made operational failures more frequent, higher-impact and more opaque, while traditional incident response remains human-centric and fragile: manual correlation of siloed metrics/logs/traces across disparate dashboards, static and quickly outdated runbooks, escalation dependent on tribal knowledge, signal overload during major incidents, and a resulting human bottleneck with hero culture and on-call fatigue (Abstract, p. 1; §I, p. 1; §II, p. 2). These detection and diagnosis delays prolong outages and make remediation quality inconsistent (§I, p. 1), and existing AIOps tools remain largely advisory — symptom detection and alert correlation without end-to-end causal reasoning, policy-aware planning or guarded execution (§II and Table I, p. 2).

AIDR-Cloud, an agentic incident detection-and-response framework explicitly positioned as an 'agentic SRE co-pilot' rather than a purely advisory AIOps tool (§I, p. 2; Abstract, p. 1). It has a three-layer architecture (§III, Fig. 1, pp. 2-3): a Perception Layer ingesting metrics, logs and traces with threshold/statistical anomaly detection; a Cognition Layer of five role-specialized collaborating LLM agents — Detector (groups anomalies into candidate incidents), Hypothesis (proposes candidate root causes), Validator (tests hypotheses against observability/cloud-API evidence with confidence scores), Planner (synthesizes ordered remediation plans with pre/postconditions, risk levels and rollback conditions) and Critic/Governance (reviews plans against policy, deciding autonomous vs. human-approval vs. advisory execution) — reasoning over a Neo4j cloud knowledge graph of services, regions, gateways, topics, databases and their dependency/failover edges (§III, p. 3; §IV, p. 3); and an Action Layer executing guarded, idempotent remediation via Kubernetes, cloud-provider, mesh/gateway and Kafka APIs with closed-loop telemetry feedback (§III, p. 3). A cross-cutting safety and governance framework enforces hard limits, canary rollouts, auto-rollback and explicit operator approval for high-risk operations such as region-wide failover (§III, p. 3). Agents use GPT-5 or Claude-Opus class models via tool-augmented prompts, orchestrated by a Go serverless layer, integrated with Prometheus, cloud logs and tracing; deployment starts in shadow/assist mode and graduates to autonomous execution of low-risk actions (§IV, p. 3).

Three complementary evaluation axes (Abstract, p. 1; §V, p. 4). (1) Controlled fault-injection experiments on a multi-region Kubernetes + Kafka environment using Chaos Mesh and custom scripts (node outages, control-plane degradation, Kafka lag spikes, data-store throttling, gateway under-scaling, cross-region latency spikes), with multiple independent runs per fault type in a baseline configuration — experienced SREs using standard observability dashboards and runbooks — versus a treatment configuration with AIDR-Cloud as primary responder and humans in oversight; measured outcomes: MTTD, MTTR, RCA latency, RCA correctness vs. ground truth, remediation success, escalation beyond approval gates, and manual operator actions, under comparable traffic conditions (§V.A, p. 4). (2) A declared statistical methodology: bootstrap two-sided 95% confidence intervals, paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, effect sizes, and an a priori power analysis (§V.B, p. 4) — though the paper states precise run counts and CIs 'can be reported in tabular form' without actually tabulating them. (3) Cost/latency decomposition into perception, cognition and action components with an LLM token-based cost model (§V.D, Table II, pp. 4-5), plus a multi-week hybrid-mode production deployment comparing AIDR-Cloud-assisted vs. human-only real incidents and postmortem quality (§V.E, p. 5).

Executed empirical comparison against a concrete human-SRE baseline (Art. I satisfied). Synthetic fault-injection: MTTR falls 'from a baseline on the order of tens of minutes to single-digit minutes in many cases', with bootstrap CIs for the difference in means excluding zero, RCA explanations reached 'several times faster' than humans, tighter MTTR distributions (less variance), and statistically and practically significant reductions in MTTR and RCA latency (§V.C, p. 4). Production deployment (Table III, §V.E, p. 5): MTTD p90 reduced from 30 min pre-deployment to 5 min with AIDR-Cloud (-83%); MTTR p90 reduced from 240 min to 20 min (-91%). Aggregate conclusion figures (§VIII, p. 6): MTTR reduced by approximately 63%, root-cause analysis accelerated ~3x, human escalations decreased 65%, correct remediations selected in roughly 70% of scenarios, with no unsafe actions executed. Overhead: cognition adds reasoning latency on the order of seconds versus minutes of recovery time saved (§V.D, p. 4; §VI, p. 5), at an LLM cost of $0.079 +/- $0.024 per incident (12,400 +/- 3,200 input tokens, 2,800 +/- 890 output tokens; Table II, p. 5). Note the paper reports -63% as the overall MTTR reduction (§VIII) alongside the -91% p90 figure for real incidents (Table III); exact per-scenario synthetic values are described qualitatively, not tabulated.

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: Demonstrates a complete perception-cognition-action agentic loop in production-grade cloud operations: role-specialized LLM agents (Detector/Hypothesis/Validator/Planner/Critic) grounded in a domain knowledge graph for explicit causal reasoning, with guarded closed-loop actuation — advancing beyond advisory AIOps recommendation engines (Table I and §II, p. 2). Shows that a layered safety and governance framework (policy engine, canary, auto-rollback, tiered human approval, full audit logging) can make partial autonomy safe, with zero unsafe actions reported (Abstract, p. 1; §III, p. 3; §VIII, p. 6). Contributes a reusable cost/latency accounting template for agentic systems (token-level cost model, seconds of reasoning overhead traded for minutes of MTTR; §V.D, pp. 4-5) and evidence of a virtuous feedback loop in which agent participation enriches the knowledge graph, runbooks and postmortems over time (§V.E, p. 5; §VI, pp. 5-6). Frames agentic AI as 'a statistically well-characterized and cost-conscious SRE co-pilot' (Abstract, p. 1).

Acknowledged limitations (§VI, pp. 5-6): hypotheses are incomplete or overly narrow for novel failure modes or external dependencies not represented in the knowledge graph, so human expertise remains essential; reliance on observability means missing or misleading telemetry creates blind spots; organizations with very high incident volumes or strict cost constraints must calibrate LLM usage (mixing high-capability and lighter models or rules). Reviewer-noted reporting gaps: despite the declared statistical rigor, precise run counts, confidence intervals and per-scenario synthetic numbers are never tabulated (§V.B-V.C, p. 4), the real-incident comparison is pre/post rather than randomized (Table III, p. 5), and the single-organization, vendor-authored deployment (Intuit; §IV, p. 3) limits external validity. Future work (§VII, p. 6): reinforcement learning or retrieval-augmented prompting to learn from historical incidents; broader incident taxonomy and graph coverage (serverless functions, batch pipelines, third-party and cross-organizational dependencies); evolution from reactive responder to proactive risk forecasting and preemptive mitigation; standardized schemas for inter-organizational sharing of anonymized incident learnings.

Directly on-construct: the paper's own framing is an agentic 'SRE co-pilot' that reduces detection and recovery times in cloud incident response (Abstract, p. 1; §VIII, p. 6), matching the thesis object (agentic copilot reducing MTTD/MTTR in incident response). It is one of the four primary studies in the first cluster that report nominal MTTD/MTTR values against an executed concrete baseline (experienced human SREs with dashboards and runbooks, §V.A, p. 4; Table III, p. 5), satisfying RSL Art. I for comparative-benefit claims, and it adds rare production-deployment evidence plus per-incident cost accounting useful to the thesis's feasibility argument. It enters the corpus with the mandatory stratum caveat: the IEEE SOUTHEASTCON series is a B2-stratum venue, so inclusion carries the qualification formalized in PDR-0006/0007.

High — it provides exactly the evidence class the thesis needs: nominal MTTD/MTTR deltas (MTTD p90 -83%, MTTR p90 -91% in production, Table III, p. 5; ~-63% MTTR overall, §VIII, p. 6) from an executed comparison against a human-SRE baseline, for an explicitly co-pilot-framed agentic system. The score is tempered only by the B2 venue stratum (mandatory caveat per PDR-0006/0007) and by incomplete tabulation of the declared statistics, not by relevance.
